## Chapter 27: Value Stream Mapping

### What Is Value Stream Mapping?

Value stream mapping is a pictorial representation, including the addition of numerical data, of the value stream for a product or for ideas. When used correctly, value stream mapping gives Six Sigma teams the big picture of a process, lets teams understand what the process looks like today, helps teams build a vision for improving a process, and connects the flow of materials, people, and information into a single image. A value stream map also helps break down communication barriers, because the symbology used tends to be similar, or at least intuitive; that makes it easier for teams and support staff to understand where waste — or muda — is occurring in a process.

### Assessing the Seven Flows

A value stream map is one of the few tools that actually captures the entire flow occurring in a process. It's possible to capture some information about all seven main types of flow on a value stream map, though most value stream maps focus more on raw material, parts, and products than on the other four flow types. The seven types of flow are:

- People
- Raw material
- Parts
- Products
- Equipment
- Information
- Engineering

### Value Stream Map Symbology

Value stream maps use different symbols than most process maps, and the symbols tend to be more specific. For example, if the value stream involves delivering goods by truck, the map includes an actual picture of a truck — usually with a text note showing how many times shipments occur in a given period.

The image above indicates one truck shipment per week. Several other common value stream map symbols are included below. You can download common symbols for Excel at www.lean.org/common/display/?o=866, to build value stream maps in Excel. You can also use value stream mapping software to build a map.

Note that value stream mapping doesn't require the exact use of these symbols, especially if you're using the value stream mapping concept in a sector where such symbols are less useful. You could use the value stream concept to map workflow in an emergency-room department, for example, where different symbols would make more sense. Think of these symbols as a starting point.

The manufacturing process box indicates a specific action in the production process. The action's name goes at the top of the box — in this case, "Press." At the bottom, you can add text notes or illustrations as desired. A common use for the process box's lower section is to indicate how much time that specific step takes.

External sources are suppliers or customers. Use this shape to indicate when inputs come from outside the organization or process, or when outputs go to the process's end customer.

Data boxes matter because they hold the value stream map's analytical content. Information commonly logged in data boxes includes:

- **Cycle Time, or C/T.** Cycle time is how long it takes for the process as a whole — or a step within the process — to complete one iteration.
- **Changeover Time, C/O.** Changeover time is how long a shift, tool, or other resource change takes in the process, or in a single step within the process.
- Number of operators
- Number of shifts
- Time worked in a shift
- First-pass yield quality
- Batch sizes
- **Takt time**, the rate at which products need to be finished to meet customer demand. Takt time for an individual process step can be thought of as the time that step needs to be completed in, so it doesn't delay the process.

The inventory box indicates that inventory tends to build up at a given point in the process. It's usually accompanied by text noting how much inventory is on hand, in quantity, time, or both. You might note there are regularly 100 parts of inventory at that point in the process. You might note there are two days of inventory at that point in the process; you could note both.

A push arrow indicates that something — product or information — is pushed from one part of the process to another. The push arrow means the product or information is generated by that part of the process, regardless of whether it's needed by the downstream parts of the process.

The opposite of a push arrow would be a pull indicator, which means downstream processes pull inventory, parts, or information as needed from upstream locations.

The finished-goods arrow indicates the process's output is being pushed or delivered to the customer — whether that customer is internal, external, or another process.

The FIFO arrow indicates that part of the process runs a "first-in, first-out" sequence, which matters in some processes. Consider processes dealing with food ingredients; if a recipe at a manufacturing plant calls for milk, operators need to pull the oldest (still good) milk from stock first, to avoid wasting product that spoils while sitting in inventory.

The supermarket is an area of the process where small amounts of inventory are stored. Downstream processes can draw from the supermarket as needed, instead of drawing from the larger stock, which might be harder to access. An upstream process feeds the supermarket, making sure there's enough inventory stocked. An example of a supermarket can be seen in a large office. A team might have a drawer where supplies, like paper, pens, clips, and staples, are kept. The team can pull from that drawer, instead of requisitioning from the larger supply room or the actual office-supply store every time they need supplies.

The physical pull symbol indicates that the product or material has to be physically pulled from the previous step, station, or supermarket to the next step.

The forklift movement symbol is self-explanatory, though it isn't always needed in every process. You might, however, have a symbol for other types of movement, like hand-truck or conveyor-belt movement. The only time you need to include specifics about how items are moved is when those details might matter for the process analysis.

This is also a self-explanatory symbol, and it isn't needed in every process either. You could instead have shipments by train, plane, or even bicycle listed on your value stream map.

The type of information indicated by the straight manual-flow arrow is typically communicated via memos, face-to-face conversation, phone calls, and reports. The manual information arrow might come with notes about the type of information and how often it's delivered.

The bent electronic-information-flow arrow indicates information of an electronic nature, such as information communicated via the Internet, portals, EDI, and automated reporting systems. The data type and how often it's delivered can also be included with this symbol.

The withdrawal kanban shape indicates there's a kanban card or signal at that process step. The kanban card instructs the operator at that specific step to pull inventory from a supermarket or other stock location.

The production kanban shape indicates a production kanban card or signal is located at that part of the process. That card tells the operator to produce a certain quantity of parts, to feed a downstream process.

The safety-stock icon indicates there's "just in case" inventory storage at that point in the process. Safety stock isn't like a supermarket — it isn't meant to be permanent inventory storage. Instead, it's temporary inventory storage that reduces the chance that stoppages or other upstream issues will prevent all the downstream processes from happening. For example, at a fast-food restaurant, someone restocks the cup and drink dispenser every morning. Those stocks aren't meant to be the permanent storage for those items, but a smaller number of items are kept on hand, so employees can quickly provide drinks to customers.

The operator shape indicates a human operator or employee within the process. You don't need to include the operator shape in every diagram where people are present — in some cases, the nature of the value stream map lets readers assume people are part of the process. However, if automated processes are included in the middle of people-driven processes, this symbol can be used to add clarity where needed.

The schedule box is simply a text box that lets you note how work, orders, or other parts of the process are scheduled. You can combine the box with arrows to show that orders are sent weekly, for example, or that a production schedule for the team is created every month.

### Value Stream Mapping Tips

Building a value stream map is very different from building a process map. One of the points of value stream mapping is that it forces you to actually experience the process, meaning building value stream maps by committee won't produce the best result. The whole team can get involved in value stream mapping, if you, as a Six Sigma practitioner, find that valuable, but the best results often come when each person starts with their own individual value stream map. This is also a good process for the Six Sigma practitioners on a team, because it forces each of them to see the process individually.

While you can use the icons above and various software programs to build a final copy of your value stream map, use pen and paper for your first drafts. That lets you log information as you walk through the process, quickly changing it as you go.

When building process maps, you often focus on the process, the employees, and the requirements. When building value stream maps, you should always focus mainly on the customer and the product.

Physically walk the process whenever possible, instead of sitting at a computer or working in a brainstorming session. Some experts recommend walking the process backward; others say to start from the beginning — find the method that works best for you. Don't try to map every part of the process, especially if you're mapping a large-scale production process. Instead, follow the main raw materials through to the outputs. If you put every process on a single map, it becomes too hard to read, and you lose the tool's value.

While you might eventually build a desired future-state value stream map, start by mapping the way things are. Even if you see they aren't working, log the actual process. Use real-time data for the value stream map whenever possible. For example, don't use historical production and changeover times; when you walk the process, use a stopwatch to log your own observations.

**VSM with digital data.** The principle above ("use real-time data, not historical times") is exactly what current digital-VSM practice automates: instead of the manual stopwatch, the same MES/ERP/IoT sensor already described in Chapter 105 feeds the value stream map with continuously updated cycle times, WIP, and lead time, and Power BI dashboards replace periodic paper-map updates with an always-current view of the current state. This doesn't replace the physical walk through the process (gemba) recommended above — the market-practice consensus is that digital VSM *amplifies* classic VSM, not replaces it: the map still provides the flow's design intent, while the digital infrastructure provides continuous measurement and control. For the **future-state** map, this means cycle-time and WIP targets can be compared against real-time actual data, instead of waiting for the next manual collection round.

### Steps in Value Stream Mapping

Start value stream mapping by selecting the product family or process you're concerned with. In a manufacturing setting, you might select product type C and only worry about that product. For example, a toy factory might make dolls, dollhouses, and toy cars, but the Six Sigma team might only be concerned with the dollhouses. In fact, the Six Sigma team might only be concerned with the doors made for the dollhouses — you decide what value stream map scope makes sense for your project.

Next, gather as much relevant data as possible about the process's current state. Do this by walking the process and taking notes, reviewing actual data, and talking with subject-matter experts.

### Build a Value Stream Map Drawing

To build a sample value stream map while we walk through the following steps, let's consider a simple real-world example. In our example, a factory makes crayons. The Six Sigma team is concerned with the process that makes the box of 8 primary-color crayons.

The value stream map will need to include information like:

- The raw-material suppliers (wax, dye, and paper)
- Melting the wax
- Adding the dye
- Pouring into molds to create the crayon shapes
- Inspection points
- Wrapping the crayons with the appropriate paper
- Packing the crayons into boxes of eight
- Shipping to the end customer — in this case, retail stores
- Start with the main process steps in the value stream. These are shown by process boxes and are joined in a line from left to right by the appropriate arrows — often push arrows. For our example process, let's assume some basic process steps:
   a. Wax is melted and dye is added
   b. Wax is poured into molds
   c. Molds are emptied
   d. Inspection happens
   e. Molded crayons are wrapped with the matching-color paper
   f. Crayons are packed into boxes
   g. Shipping

Above, you can see a rough sketch of the process portion of the value stream map. Kanban cards or signals tell employees when to pull wax and dye from the supermarket inventory. (The signal might be a light indicating the previous batch was processed and the machines returned to the process's starting parameters). Employees add the ingredients and start the first part of the process, which is automated after the initial ingredient measurements. The wax is melted, the dye is mixed in, the colored wax is poured into molds, and the mold sits for 10 minutes before the crayons are emptied out to the inspection station.

You'll notice the arrows connecting the first processes are different, because we want to show they're automated and the process just flows together, unless someone intervenes on that batch. The rest of the processes have push arrows, because inspection, adding paper, and packing don't run in a batch process and work as long as inventory is flowing.

1. Add the important aspects outside the process, including process controls, supplies, customers, and shipments.

1. Add data boxes for each part of the process.

1. Add inventory signals and any other information you consider relevant to the value stream map. For example, when reviewing the crayon process used in the example, the Six Sigma practitioner might notice that inventory builds up before the packing process, because it's slower than the inspection and paper-wrapping processes. That could be indicated with an inventory signal and text.

You can also add controls for the process. In this case, the retailer places orders a month in advance, noting how many boxes it'll need each week in the following month. The crayon-manufacturing company builds a monthly forecast, but places weekly orders with suppliers. Suppliers deliver in several batches a week. Production control manages each part of the process with scheduling, to keep up with retailer demands.

Finally, add a timeline at the bottom, noting how long it takes for a single item to move through the entire process, splitting the time into value-added and non-value-added.

In the example above, the yellow parts are value-added. They represent the time the product is actually being made or changed. The white parts are setup, lead times, and inventory waiting times — and this particular process is for a single crayon color, and doesn't account for any time spent prepping the machines for a color changeover.

You can add up the times to see the total process time is 194 minutes, or 3.23 hours. The value-added time is 19 minutes, so the team can assume there's definitely waste that can be removed from this process.

Remember, value stream maps shouldn't be formal documents — they're working representations of the process, to help you and the rest of a Six Sigma team better understand the process and related challenges. So, you can add as much or as little information as you find necessary. You can also go back and add information later, if needed. The first draft of a value stream map, whether using pen and paper or a computer program, will probably end up messy, and that's fine. In fact, that's a sign you're doing it right. You can always make a clean final copy for inclusion in presentations and training documents, if desired.

**Process timeline (summary)**

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Total process time (lead time) | 194 minutes (≈ 3.23 hours) |
| Value-added time | 19 minutes |
| % value-added of total | ≈ 9.8% |

*The big gap between total time and value-added time is the classic sign that there's waste (waiting, idle stock, changeover times) to be removed from the process — exactly the kind of opportunity value stream mapping exists to reveal. This summary replaces the old yellow/white time "ruler" with a table, which is easier to read.*

### What to Do with Value Stream Maps?

Value stream mapping is a useful tool for every DMAIC phase. During the Define phase, value stream mapping as an activity forces you to engage with the process at a physical, day-to-day level, which can deepen your understanding of the process you're working to improve. It also gives the whole team another visual resource that helps when discussing the process and the problem. A good value stream map lets the team visualize exactly where the process and the problem might occur relative to overall production.

Building a value stream map means you've already done some measurement, creating a baseline for the Measure phase. The value stream map also points to measurement and data-collection points that can be used later in the Measure phase, though teams should never limit themselves to only the first types of information gathered during value stream mapping.

During the Analyze phase, value stream maps are a tool that helps teams brainstorm and identify root causes or problem points in a process, and you can use the initial value stream map to identify activities or resources that don't add value — the ones creating muda in the process. Finally, during the Improve phase, teams can start building a future-state value stream map, building on the old map and using the information and solutions they developed throughout the DMAIC process. By putting those solutions on paper in the form of a value stream map, teams can better understand where problems might arise and adjust the solutions accordingly, to reduce the number of problems faced during and after implementation.

### Tips for Building a Future-State Value Stream Map

1. Use the current-state value stream map and all the other information gathered and analyzed, to identify as many sources of waste in the process as possible.
2. Categorize the waste into two types: waste resulting from remote locations, machinery, and product designs, all of which are necessary elements for the final product, and waste that doesn't result from those things.
3. Focus on the second type of waste and build a future-state value stream map that removes it all.
4. Review the future-state map to make sure the processes can flow properly. Ask yourself questions like:
   a. What's the takt time needed at each station to meet overall demand, and can every process step meet that takt time? If not, the team might need to address the steps that can't.
   b. How will production be scheduled? There's usually a specific part of the process that controls the production schedule. Ultimately, the best and most optimal control is by the customer (the customer needs 100 a day, so the process should make 100 a day). However, there are times when a specific part of the process is only capable of X units per time period, and the team can't change that capacity because of resource constraints or other reasons. If the process isn't controlled by that "pacemaker step," then inventory will build up ahead of it.
   c. Is batch processing needed, or can it be removed?
   d. What process changes and improvements are needed to implement the future-state value stream? Sometimes, machinery changes, staffing changes, or capital investments are needed, and they aren't always possible. Before moving ahead with future-state plans, Six Sigma teams have to make sure resources will be approved and available.

As with anything in Lean and Six Sigma processes, the value stream map isn't a requirement. In fact, one of the cardinal rules of value stream mapping is not to map just to map. Yes, a finished, polished map looks nice — and can be especially impressive in presentations or documents, when other people in the organization aren't fully familiar with the tool. However, if building a value stream map won't help a Six Sigma team in any of the DMAIC phases, or if the process involved simply doesn't lend itself to that kind of mapping, then skip this tool. A Six Sigma practitioner should always be aware that muda can creep into any process — and that includes the process of assessing and improving something. If you're building a value stream map for no reason, then you're creating overproduction muda.
